name: Kapwing
tagline: Browser video, image, and meme editing with AI and team workflows

pricing.notes: Working normalization from the official public pricing structure. Recheck the source page immediately before publication.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 10 credits; 30 export minutes/month; 4-minute videos; 720p watermarked; 2 GB uploads; projects retained 3 days
tiers.notes: Official page gives conflicting text-to-speech caps in different comparison rows.

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.limits: 1,000 credits/month; 2-hour exports; 4K; 6 GB uploads; 100 GB storage; 1,000 subtitle minutes/month

tiers.name: Business
tiers.limits: 4,000 credits/month; 500 GB storage; 4,000 subtitle minutes; 200 dubbing minutes; 2,000 translation minutes/month

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom credits, storage, security, support and procurement

pricing.freeTierCaps: 10 credits, 30 export minutes/month, 4-minute maximum video, 720p watermarked exports, 2 GB uploads and 3-day project retention
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; subscriptions auto-renew and published policy says payments are non-refundable
pricing.hiddenCosts: AI tools consume credits at different rates; free projects are deleted after 3 days, and every paid collaborator is a separate paid member.

verdictSummary: The visible collaborative video editor loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. Kapwing earns its keep through media pipeline, hosting, distribution, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a local collaborative video editor workflow that imports user-owned media, applies the core edit or transformation, previews it, and exports a standard file.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
requirements: optional model or API key in .env
whatYouLose: high-fidelity color, format, and export handling
whyPeopleStillPay: Kapwing: People pay to avoid codec failures, upload limits, rendering surprises, lost recordings, and distribution chores.
ongoingBurden: Maintain codecs, media probing, resumable processing, storage cleanup, exports, device permissions, and performance.

alternatives.name: Adobe Express
alternatives.desc: Browser video, images, captions, graphics and memes without a watermark; team niceties remain paid.

alternatives.name: Clipchamp
alternatives.desc: A capable browser editor with free 1080p exports; image-and-meme work is much thinner than Kapwing.

rejectedAlternatives.name: OpenCut
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The famous answer is between codebases: classic is archived and the replacement is still a rewrite.

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of Kapwing is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for Kapwing, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Python 3.12 + FastAPI + FFmpeg + React.
Primary job: Build a local collaborative video editor workflow that imports user-owned media, applies the core edit or transformation, previews it, and exports a standard file.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: distribution and podcast hosting; professional codecs, effects, and collaboration; high-fidelity color, format, and export handling.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
